Botch
BOCH
noun
From Middle English bocche, a swelling, boil, or ulcerous sore, akin to Old French boce (a bump or swelling). The Hebrew is sh’chin, an inflamed boil or ulcer. In the KJV it names “the botch of Egypt,” the incurable sore of the covenant curse.

Biblical Definition

A botch is a large inflamed boil or ulcerous sore, and in Scripture it is fixed as the very signature of Egypt’s plague turned back upon a covenant-breaking people. Twice in the great catalogue of curses Moses names it. The LORD will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods , and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed (Deu 28:27); and again, the LORD shall smite thee in the knees, and in the legs, with a sore botch that cannot be healed, from the sole of thy foot unto the top of thy head (Deu 28:35). The phrase “the botch of Egypt” is deliberate and dreadful: the plague once loosed on Israel’s oppressors becomes, if Israel apostatizes, the plague loosed on Israel. What God did to Pharaoh He will not scruple to do to a rebellious son. The boil breaking forth with blains (Exo 9:9) was the botch upon Egypt; here the same running sore covers the disobedient covenant-people from sole to crown, incurable by any hand. Herein lies the terror and the mercy of the covenant: its blessings are unspeakable and its curses are exact, and no man who has felt the botch cleaving to him from foot to head can imagine his sin a small thing. Yet the curse points beyond itself, for the sores which no physician could heal were borne at last by One made a curse for us, upon whom the chastisement of our peace was laid.

Webster 1828 Definition

A large inflamed boil, ulcer, or eruptive sore upon the body.

expand to see more

BOTCH, n. [Middle Eng. bocche, a swelling; Old Fr. boce, a bump.] A swelling or eruptive sore upon the skin; an ulcer; a large inflamed boil.

In Scripture, the botch of Egypt, the grievous boil of the sixth plague, named among the incurable curses of the covenant (Deut. xxviii. 27, 35).

A sore covering the body from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, that cannot be healed by the art of man.

By extension, any foul ulcerous eruption, the outward mark of a wasting and shameful disease.

Figuratively, a clumsy or corrupt patching of a thing, as to botch a work; a mending that only mars.

Key Scripture

Deu 28:27 — "The LORD will smite thee with the botch of Egypt, and with the emerods , and with the scab, and with the itch, whereof thou canst not be healed."

Deu 28:35 — "The LORD shall smite thee in the knees, and in the legs, with a sore botch that cannot be healed, from the sole of thy foot unto the top of thy head."

Exo 9:9 — "And it shall become small dust in all the land of Egypt, and shall be a boil breaking forth with blains upon man, and upon beast, throughout all the land of Egypt."

Deu 28:21 — "The LORD shall make the pestilence cleave unto thee, until he have consumed thee from off the land, whither thou goest to possess it."

Modern Corruption

Not a disputed doctrine but a covenant curse; it recovers the exactness of God’s judgments and the incurableness of sin apart from Christ.

expand to see more

The age treats the covenant as a soft thing, all blessing and no sanction, and it recoils from a God who names the precise sore He will send upon the disobedient, from the sole of the foot to the top of the head. But the botch of Egypt was set into the covenant on purpose. What the LORD did to the oppressor He warned He would do to His own people should they turn to Egypt’s idols and hardness—the same running, incurable ulcer, no longer against Pharaoh but against a rebellious son. To forget the sanctions is to forget how seriously God takes the vows of His people; the curses are the measure of the covenant’s weight.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sin is an incurable sore whereof no man can heal himself, and that the covenant which threatens the botch also provides the remedy. The chastisement that would cover the guilty from foot to crown fell instead upon the Surety, who was wounded for our transgressions—the only physician of a disease no physician could touch. The curse is exact; so is the grace that answers it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A word for an ulcerous boil rooted in the Middle English for a swelling.

expand to see more

Middle English bocche—a swelling, boil, or ulcer; kin to Old French boce, a bump or protuberance.

Hebrew sh’chin—an inflamed boil or burning ulcer, the sore of the sixth plague.

“The botch of Egypt”—a fixed phrase in Deuteronomy 28, the plague of the oppressor turned against the covenant-breaker.

An incurable sore, covering the body from the sole of the foot to the top of the head, past the reach of any physician.

A second, homely sense survives—to botch a work, to patch it clumsily; a mending that mars, from the same idea of a lumpish swelling.

Usage

"The botch of Egypt was written into the covenant curses, that Israel might not presume upon the blessings."

"A sore botch from foot to crown—the incurableness of the disease preached the incurableness of sin apart from grace."

"No physician could heal the botch; only the Surety made a curse for us could bear it away."
